name: Chalisa famine
summary: Named for Vikram Samvat 1840. Drought from Delhi through the Doab, Awadh, Punjab, Rajputana and Kashmir, on Company, Awadh and Maratha ground. The southern dearth of 1782–83 had already sat on Madras. Where the Company collected, it collected. Grain still moved. Grove’s later figure of about eleven million covers this famine and that southern dearth together; it is not a register.
scaleRationale: A North Indian famine on Company and Maratha ground; later writers treat it as one of the great mortalities of the 1780s, without a census.

parties.note: Maratha and Awadh zones sat inside the drought as well as Company ground.

name: Doji bara famine
summary: Four failed monsoons. In Bijapur the unburied whitened the roads. In Hyderabad the kotwal counted ninety thousand bodies carried out in four months, and the amildars still tried to collect. Madras banned Tanjore rice for export except to the starving districts, imported from Bengal, and fed a few thousand on porridge. Grove’s eleven million for 1789–92 is an order of magnitude, not a census.
scaleRationale: Deccan, Hyderabad, Gujarat, Marwar and the Northern Circars; Company Madras kept the only systematic files.

resources.note: Madras moved Bengal rice north and stopped Tanjore export except to the distressed districts.

parties.note: Southern Maratha country; Peshwa grain doles at Poona did not reach Bijapur.

name: Orissa famine of 1866
summary: Na'anka: the ninth anka of the Puri king. Rice left for Britain while Orissa starved. Beadon would not touch the market. The Campbell Commission named the failure. Official dead in the division about a million, a third of the population; the Gazetteer’s wider band is four to five million. Not a single integer.
scaleRationale: A named colonial failure of relief; a third of coastal Orissa dead on the official count, and a multi-million band for the east-coast famine as a whole.

resources.note: Naoroji: more than 200 million pounds of rice exported from India in the famine year.

legalRegimes.name: Laissez-faire grain trade, Bengal Presidency
legalRegimes.note: Beadon refused to regulate prices; the Board of Revenue trusted fictitious lists until the monsoon closed the ports.

name: Rajputana famine of 1868–70
summary: After Orissa, Muir told every district officer he would answer for a starvation death. Relief works sat in Ajmer. The princely states spent almost nothing. Two-thirds of Marwar walked. Grain still had to come in on camels. The Gazetteer put the dead over a million and a half. Brooke’s working count was lower. Contested.
scaleRationale: Rajputana, Ajmer, Agra and the Hissar tract; a famine of emigration as much as of camps.

legalRegimes.name: Muir’s starvation-responsibility order, 1868
legalRegimes.note: Written after Orissa: every district officer personally responsible that no avoidable starvation death occurred.

name: Indian famine of 1896–97
summary: Bundelkhand first, then the Central Provinces, the Deccan, Madras. Ganjam and Vizagapatam kept exporting grain. The Famine Code made a camp and a wage. Official British-territory dead about a million; Visaria and Maharatna, working the censuses, four and a half to five. Lyall’s commission of 1898 kept the Code and tightened the tests. Lytton’s Temple wage was still in the file.
scaleRationale: A multi-presidency famine; official dead in the millions’ floor, later demography several times that.

resources.note: Sea- and rail-borne grain left Ganjam and Vizagapatam throughout the famine year.

peoples.name: United Provinces and Central Provinces peasantry

legalRegimes.name: Provisional Famine Code, 1883
legalRegimes.note: Relief as camp and wage; tribal groups in Chota Nagpur were judged to have forest produce and so fell outside charitable relief.

name: Indian famine of 1899–1900
summary: Chhappania Kal. The country had not recovered from 1896. Wheat and cotton still left Bombay. Curzon cut rations he called dangerously high and brought back the Temple tests. Relief camps filled; cholera and then monsoon malaria emptied them. Official about a million in British districts; Maharatna three to four and a half. MacDonnell’s commission of 1901 wrote the last all-India famine of the Victorian codes.
scaleRationale: Bombay, the Central Provinces, Ajmer, Rajputana and Gujarat; the last all-India famine of the Crown Raj.

resources.note: Davis: wheat and cotton still exported through Bombay — dearth amidst plenty.
